axis_note: E-path, but an atypical instance and the earliest one in this corpus. E here holds the model's own internal (key, value) activations, not text/vector/graph records, and it is read by an attention head rather than spliced into the prompt. It therefore sits functionally where W sits (inside the forward pass, at one layer, mixed into the residual stream by a learned gate) while having E's storage semantics (outside the parameters, non-differentiable, unbounded, per-document, clearable). The monograph should place it as the E-path's representation-level ancestor: the paper that established that a non-differentiable external store read by attention beats making the differentiable context bigger, four years before the agent-memory line rediscovered the same argument in text space.

problem_stated.one_line: Acquiring new knowledge currently requires moving Theta (train or finetune); the paper proposes acquiring it instead by writing into a non-differentiable external store at inference time, read back by attention.

verbatim_anchors.quote: Language models typically need to be trained or finetuned in order to acquire new knowledge, which involves updating their weights. We instead envision language models that can simply read and memorize new data at inference time, thus acquiring new knowledge immediately.
transformer performance on many of these tasks is limited by the context length of attention, which is typically short.

Attention over long sequences is also useful as a form of rapid learning. Facts and information which are stored in the form of weight matrices must be slowly trained over hundreds of thousands of training steps. By using attention, however, a model can simply memorize facts (e.g. function definitions) by storing them as (key, value) pairs in long-term memory, and then retrieve those facts later by creating a query that attends to them. In this case, attention acts as a form of information retrieval, allowing the model to look up facts that it has seen previously.

gradients are not backpropagated into the external memory, which is critical to the scalability of our technique. The keys and values are a function of model parameters, so attempting to backpropagate gradients into external memory would necessarily involve computing all of the keys and values with the current model parameters on every training step. However, if the external memory is not differentiable, then we can instead instead reuse keys and values that were previously computed on prior training steps, which drastically reduces the amount of computation for large memories.

verbatim_anchors.quote: unlike some other approaches, kNN lookup does not do averaging or summarization of tokens at long distances, but retrieves exact values even from the distant context.

problem_stated.framing_metaphor: Attention as information retrieval. The paper repeatedly identifies attention-over-memory with IR ('attention acts as a form of information retrieval', line 39; 'a simple model that unifies attention and retrieval', line 202), and identifies weights with slow storage ('stored in the form of weight matrices must be slowly trained', lines 36-37). This is the Theta-vs-E tradeoff stated explicitly in March 2022, with no sleep/consolidation vocabulary anywhere in the paper (zero occurrences of 'sleep', 'consolidat', 'replay', 'catastrophic', 'continual').

inherited_open_question.detail: The paper inherits no quoted open question from any prior work. Sec. 2 (Related Work, lines 93-205) is a positioning survey written entirely in the third person and the present tense; it contains no quotation, no 'X leaves open', no 'as asked by', and no restatement of anyone's future-work paragraph. Every comparison is a contrast the authors draw themselves ('In contrast, we use a very large cache without compression', line 183; '(We use kNN lookup to approximate attention to previous tokens, not to replace the FFN.)', lines 190-191; 'Instead, we focus on language modeling using a decoder-only model', line 201).

what_it_implicitly_answers.question: Transformer-XL (Dai et al. 2019) and Compressive Transformer (Rae et al. 2020) both carry a non-differentiable cache across steps. How far can such a cache be scaled, and must the carried state be compressed?
what_it_implicitly_answers.answer_given: To 262K (key, value) pairs, and no: compression is unnecessary if you replace dense attention over the cache with approximate top-k_nn retrieval.
what_it_implicitly_answers.source: Sec. 2 lines 113-124 (the description of truncated BPTT -> neural caches -> Transformer-XL -> Rae et al.), Sec. 2 line 183, Table 5 (lines 510-561)

what_it_implicitly_answers.question: Sun et al. (2021), 'Do long-range language models actually use long-range context?', is the standing negative result on whether long-context models exploit what they are given.
what_it_implicitly_answers.answer_given: The paper does not quote the question, but Sec. 4.6 is built as an answer to it and cites it as corroboration: 'This result is in keeping with the prior analysis of long-context Transformers on PG19 (Sun et al., 2021), which found similar lookup patterns.' It also cites Sun et al. to justify dropping the position bias on retrieved memories.
what_it_implicitly_answers.source: Sec. 4.6, lines 645-646; Sec. 3.1 Position bias, lines 281-282

what_it_implicitly_answers.question: Khandelwal et al. (2020, kNN-LM) and Yogatama et al. (2021) put a non-differentiable store at the output softmax. Can non-differentiable memory instead be placed inside the stack?
what_it_implicitly_answers.answer_given: Yes, at a single mid-to-upper attention layer, with a learned per-head gate. The paper marks the distinction itself but does not attribute the question to those authors.

inherited_open_question.why_this_matters_for_the_monograph: An un-inherited question. The paper opens by naming the Theta alternative in its first sentence ('trained or finetuned ... updating their weights', line 10) and then cites nobody at all for it: no PEFT, no adapter, no continual-learning, no model-editing, no catastrophic-forgetting reference appears anywhere in the 145-entry bibliography (lines 778-923). The E-path therefore begins by defining itself against a literature it does not read. The same asymmetry persists downstream: MemGPT (2310.08560), Letta STC and the rest of the agent-memory line in this corpus do not cite this paper back (corpus-wide grep for 'Memorizing Transformer' returns only two later hits, both 2607.x).

core_mechanism.summary_one_line: One attention layer near the top of a frozen-topology decoder reads a per-document, per-head, non-differentiable FIFO store E of raw (k_t, v_t) pairs via approximate top-k_nn dot-product retrieval, and mixes that read into the local-attention output with a single learned per-head scalar gate; E is written by verbatim append of the same (k_t, v_t) the forward pass just computed, so the write costs nothing beyond the read.
core_mechanism.equation_numbering_note: The paper numbers only two equations, (1) and (2), both in Sec. 3.1 (lines 264-270). Everything else is prose. Citations below give the original number where one exists and the line range otherwise. Equation labels mt-N are this note's, not the paper's.

state_decomposition.Theta: All transformer parameters: token embeddings, 12 layers of dense self-attention + FFN (d=1024, 8 heads x 128, d_ff=4096), the T5 relative position bias used for local attention, the output softmax, and the per-head gate bias b_g of Eq. (1). Trained by outer loop only. [Sec. 3 lines 211-216; Sec. 4.2 lines 478-482; Sec. 3.1 lines 264-277]
state_decomposition.W: Empty. There is no fast-weight state in the NM sense anywhere in this paper: no inner loss, no test-time gradient, no fixed-size compressed state that is updated by a rule. The Transformer-XL cache (previous step's k,v prepended, sliding-window causal mask) is a bounded lossless KV carry, not W: it has no alpha_t, no S_t, and no eta_t. [Sec. 3 lines 239-242]
state_decomposition.E: Per-document, per-head FIFO of exact (k_i, v_i) pairs in R^{d_head=128}, capacity n_E = M in {1536, 8192, 65536, 131072, 262144}. Non-differentiable. Cleared at the start of each new document; one separate E per batch element. [Sec. 3.1 lines 251-255, 283-285]

E_parts.E_knn: The kNN store proper. Written at every chunk boundary, read only at the single kNN-augmented layer (layer 9 of 12 by default), only by top-k_nn retrieval. [Sec. 3.1 lines 247-261; Sec. 4.2 line 480]
E_parts.E_xl: The Transformer-XL cache: the previous chunk's (k, v) at *every* layer, prepended and attended densely under a sliding-window causal mask so each token sees the previous 512 (or 2048) tokens. Same physical content, different read rule and different residence. The paper treats these as complementary and shows additive gains. [Sec. 3 lines 239-242; Sec. 4.3 lines 573-576]

state_decomposition.what_is_NOT_in_any_layer: There is no text, no summary, no embedding of a document, no learned index, no importance score, and no consolidation step. S(c; B_s) is the identity map in representation space -- the paper's own phrasing is 'does not do averaging or summarization of tokens at long distances, but retrieves exact values' (lines 46-47) and 'we use a very large cache without compression' (line 183).

equations.label: mt-1
equations.latex: E_t \;=\; \mathrm{wr}\big(E_{t-1},\ \hat c_t\big), \qquad \hat c_t \;=\; S\big(c_t;\ B_s\big) \;=\; \big\{(k_i, v_i)\big\}_{i \in c_t}, \qquad \mathrm{wr} = \text{append-then-FIFO-evict to } n_E \le M
equations.source: [memorizing-transformers Sec. 3.1, lines 251-255] -- 'after each training step, the (key, value) pairs in the local context are appended to the end of the external memory. If the document is very long, old (key, value) pairs will be dropped from the memory to make room for new ones. Thus, for each head, the external memory keeps a cache of the prior M (key, value) pairs, where M is the memory size.'
equations.reading: This is (U-E) with S set to the identity on the chunk's own key/value activations. c_t is the chunk of C = 512 (or 2048) tokens that the forward pass just consumed; the (k_i, v_i) are exactly the tensors that attention layer already materialised. Two consequences the monograph must state: (i) the write is a by-product, so its marginal budget is zero; (ii) the time index is t, the chunk index, not k, the sleep-round index -- this is (U-E) executed synchronously at wake, never offline.

equations.label: mt-2
equations.source: [memorizing-transformers Sec. 3.1, lines 256-261; Sec. 4.2 line 480 ('we used k = 32'); Sec. 3.3 lines 311-313 ('a recall of about 90%, i.e. 90% of the true top k are returned in the approximate top k')]
equations.reading: The retrieval key space is the model's own attention key space -- the same q_t is used for local attention and for the store ('The same queries are used for both the local context, and for the external memory. The keys and values also belong to the same distribution', lines 251-252). Unlike a text-retrieval E, there is no encoder, no separate embedding model, and no similarity threshold: ret is literally the argmax of the same dot product attention already computes.

equations.label: mt-3
equations.latex: V_m \;=\; \mathrm{softmax}\big(q_t K_{\mathrm{ret}}^{\top}\big)\, V_{\mathrm{ret}}, \qquad (K_{\mathrm{ret}}, V_{\mathrm{ret}}) = \mathrm{ret}(E, q_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{k_{nn} \times d_{\mathrm{head}}}
equations.source: [memorizing-transformers Sec. 3.1, lines 256-261] -- 'we first construct an attention matrix by computing the dot product of each query against the retrieved keys, then apply softmax, and finally return a weighted sum of the retrieved values. Unlike standard dense attention, the retrieved memories contain a different set of (key, value) pairs for each query.'
equations.reading: Per-query K/V. This one sentence is the whole systems story of the paper: the K and V operands are no longer shared across the queries of a sequence, so the layer stops being a GEMM and becomes a gather. No position bias is applied here: 'We don't use a position bias for the retrieved memories' (line 280).

equations.label: mt-4
equations.reading: The gate is content-independent by construction: 'the value of the gate g does not depend on the content of the token at each position, although that would be a trivial extension to implement' (lines 275-276). It is a per-head architectural preference, learned once in the outer loop, not a routing decision made at test time.

equations.label: mt-5
equations.reading: V_c is ordinary dense attention over the local chunk plus the prepended XL cache; V_a is what continues up the residual stream. The reported outcome: 'We did observe that over time, most heads learned to attend almost exclusively to external memory' (line 277) -- i.e. sigma(b_g) -> 1 for most heads, so at convergence the kNN layer is largely an E-read layer rather than a mixture.

equations.label: mt-6
equations.latex: \hat y \;=\; f\big(q;\ \Theta,\ \varnothing,\ \mathrm{ret}(E, q)\big) \quad\text{with } \mathrm{ret} \text{ entering at exactly one layer}
equations.source: [memorizing-transformers Sec. 3.1, lines 247-250; Sec. 4.2 line 480; architecture Fig. 2, lines 126-182]
equations.reading: Standard form (R) with W = empty and the E-read injected mid-stack rather than at the input. The paper's own surprise at how little this costs: 'This is surprising, because the external memory is not differentiable, and is added only to one layer of the Transformer, whereas increasing the context size is differentiable and affects all layers. We conclude that the lower layers of a Transformer don't necessarily need long-range context, and having a differentiable memory is not as important as one might suspect.' (lines 579-582)

equations.label: mt-7
equations.latex: \text{staleness: } (k_i, v_i) = \phi(\Theta_{s(i)}) \ \ \text{with } s(i) < \text{current step}; \quad \text{mitigation: } \hat k = k/\lVert k\rVert,\ \hat q = q/\lVert q\rVert
equations.reading: During training only, E holds activations produced by *older* Theta. 'The model parameters that produce the queries change over time, and will thus have shifted since the keys and values were stored. For very large memories, older records may become "stale."' (lines 291-293). The fix is key/query normalisation (Henry et al. 2020): 'Normalization does not eliminate staleness, but it at least ensures that older keys and newer keys do not differ in magnitude.' (lines 299-301). At pure inference with frozen Theta this term vanishes -- the monograph should say so, because it is the one asymmetry between this paper's training-time and deploy-time behaviour.

outer_vs_inner.headline_for_the_reader: Nothing whatsoever is learned at test time. The only thing that moves at test time is E, and it moves by memcpy, not by gradient. Every learnable object in this paper -- including the gate that decides how much the memory matters -- is fixed by ordinary pre-training before deployment. This is the cleanest separation in the whole corpus: outer loop moves Theta, wake-time movement touches only E, and there is no third thing.

update_layer.instantiates: (U-E) only. Theta is frozen after training; W does not exist in this architecture. There is no ordering question because there is only one rule.
update_layer.canonical_form: E_{k+1} = wr(E_k, hat c_k),  hat c_k = S(c_k; B_s)

how_it_differs.difference: S is the identity, in representation space
how_it_differs.detail: hat c_t is literally {(k_i, v_i)} for the tokens of chunk c_t -- the tensors the forward pass already produced at that layer. No summarisation, no compression, no LLM call, no encoder. 'kNN lookup does not do averaging or summarization of tokens at long distances, but retrieves exact values even from the distant context' (lines 46-47); 'we use a very large cache without compression' (line 183).
how_it_differs.consequence: B_s^marginal = 0. This is the degenerate corner of the E-path and the correct reference point for costing every later E-path paper: whatever Letta STC or Mem0 spend on hat c, this paper spends nothing, and it still gets the gain. The monograph's amortisation equation (A) collapses to C_avg = C_wake here.

how_it_differs.difference: The time index is t (chunk), not k (sleep round)
how_it_differs.detail: The write fires at every chunk boundary, synchronously, inside the wake pass. There is no idle period, no separate offline job, no batching of writes.
how_it_differs.consequence: Strictly, this is not sleep-time compute under the S0 operational definition (compute spent *before* the query arrives, from a budget B_s). It is the limiting case where the sleep budget has been driven to zero by making the sleep output identical to a by-product of wake. The monograph should use it as the origin of the B_s axis, not as a point on it.

how_it_differs.difference: wr is append + FIFO eviction, with no merge, rewrite, dedup, or importance score
how_it_differs.detail: 'If the document is very long, old (key, value) pairs will be dropped from the memory to make room for new ones' (lines 253-254). There is no analogue of MemGPT's working_context.replace or Mem0's ADD/UPDATE/DELETE.
how_it_differs.consequence: E is monotone-within-window and amnesic beyond it. The paper never isolates the cost of eviction; nothing in the experiments distinguishes 'the item was evicted' from 'the item lost the top-k_nn race'.

how_it_differs.difference: E is scoped per document and per batch element, and cleared at document boundaries
how_it_differs.detail: 'Each subsequence in the batch comes from a different document, and thus requires a separate external memory, which is cleared at the start of each new document.' (lines 284-285)
how_it_differs.consequence: Amortisation is intra-document only. N_q, the number of queries sharing one context, is here the number of remaining tokens in the same document -- and the paper does report the shape of that distribution, in the appendix histograms (Figs. 9-13), which is more than any later E-path paper in this corpus does.

how_it_differs.difference: ret is dot-product top-k_nn in the model's own key space, at one layer, entering the residual stream
how_it_differs.detail: Not a prompt splice. The retrieved values are mixed into V_a by the gate (Eq. 2) at layer 9 of 12; layers 1-8 never see E.
how_it_differs.consequence: The read has no token cost. Where the text-based E-path pays for retrieval by lengthening the prompt (and thus quadratically in attention), this pays for it in a gather of k_nn=32 x d_head=128 vectors per query per head at one layer.

how_it_differs.difference: Theta is trained *with* the read in the loop, so the read is not a bolt-on
how_it_differs.detail: The gate b_g and the whole stack co-adapt to the presence of E during the 500K training steps. The paper shows the bolt-on case works too, but only after 20K-100K finetuning steps (Sec. 4.5, lines 628-635).
how_it_differs.consequence: Unlike prompt-level E, this E cannot be attached to an arbitrary frozen checkpoint for free. That is the price of putting the read inside the stack.

update_layer.layers_touched_in_order: (U-E) at every chunk boundary t, and nothing else. Theta moves only in the outer loop, before deployment. W is absent.

cost_table.preamble: This paper is a 2022 language-modelling paper and reports no serving numbers at all. Its only wall-clock measurement is a training step time, given once, in one sentence, for the smallest model. Three of the four required cells are therefore 'absent'. That absence is itself the finding: the paper that establishes the E-path's representation-level mechanism never states what it costs to serve.

B_s.value: absent as a separate quantity -- and structurally zero
B_s.detail: There is no offline pass, so there is no separable sleep budget. hat c_t is the (k, v) the wake forward pass already computed (Sec. 3.1 lines 251-253), so the marginal cost of the write is the memcpy plus index insertion, which the paper never measures. The only wall-clock figure in the paper is a *combined* read+write training step time: 'For a model with around 200M trainable parameters the step time increased from 0.2s to 0.25s when we added a memory of size 8K, and to 0.6s when we added a memory of size 65K (measured on TPUv3).' That is +25% at n_E = 8192 and 3x at n_E = 65536, and it bundles the kNN search, the extra attention, and the write together; it is a training step, not an inference step; and it is reported only at ~200M parameters.
B_s.source: Sec. 4.2, lines 496-498 (step times); Sec. 3.1, lines 251-253 (write is a by-product); Sec. 1, lines 48-52 (non-differentiability is what makes reuse of prior-step k,v possible)

L_w.detail: No inference latency, no TTFT, no ITL, no tokens/second, no decode measurement of any kind appears in the paper. The word 'latency' does not occur. The 0.2/0.25/0.6 s figures are training step times on 32 TPU cores (Sec. 4.2 line 488) at batch 2^17 tokens (lines 490-492) and cannot be read as per-token wake latency. The claim that 131K/262K memories run 'on a single TPU device, while maintaining a reasonable step time' (Sec. 1, lines 78-79) is qualitative -- 'reasonable' is never given a number.
L_w.source: Sec. 4.2, lines 488-498; Sec. 1, lines 78-79; absence throughout

C_cap.value: stated in items, never in bytes
C_cap.detail: Capacity is reported only as n_E, the number of (key, value) pairs per head per document: 1536, 8192, 65K (=65536), 131K (=131072), 262K (=262144). 'for each head, the external memory keeps a cache of the prior M (key, value) pairs, where M is the memory size' (lines 254-255). The scope is per head (8 heads), at one layer (layer 9 of 12), per document, per batch element -- 'Each subsequence in the batch comes from a different document, and thus requires a separate external memory' (lines 284-285). Head dimension is 128 (Sec. 4.2 line 479). The paper never multiplies these out, never states a dtype, and never gives a bytes figure or a per-device memory footprint. Byte capacity: absent. See systems_implications for a derived figure, explicitly marked as this note's arithmetic.
C_cap.source: Sec. 3.1, lines 253-255, 283-285; Sec. 4 line 325; Sec. 4.2 lines 478-479; Table 4 (lines 367-464); Table 5 (lines 510-561)

rho.value: absent as a number; the phenomenon is named and hedged
rho.detail: The paper has one degradation mechanism, staleness, and it is a *training-time* artifact: keys stored under older Theta drift from queries produced by newer Theta (Sec. 3.2, lines 290-306). It is never quantified. The reported symptom is hedged three times over: 'In some of our experiments, we observed that training models from scratch with a large memory sometimes resulted in worse performance than pretraining the model with a small memory of size 8192, and then finetuning it on a larger memory. This training instability could be due to staleness.' (lines 302-304); and again 'In some cases, training was unstable when using large memories, possibly due to distributional shift early in the training' (lines 599-600). No unstable run is shown anywhere in the paper. Round-over-round forgetting in the (U-Theta) sense does not apply -- Theta never moves after deployment -- and eviction-induced loss from the FIFO is never isolated.

amortization_N_q.value: collapses -- and this is the one paper in the corpus where it legitimately does
amortization_N_q.detail: Equation (A), C_avg = C_wake + C_sleep/N_q, has C_sleep = 0 here because the sleep output is a by-product of wake. There is no break-even N_q* to compute; the E-write pays for itself at N_q = 1. What the paper *does* have, and no later E-path paper in this corpus has, is the distribution of the context that N_q would be drawn from: the appendix histograms of document length (Figs. 9-13, lines 928-943), with arXiv papers up to ~1.6M tokens and Github repositories up to just over 9M tokens.
amortization_N_q.source: Sec. 3.1 lines 251-253; App. A, Figs. 9-13, lines 928-943

cost_the_paper_pays_instead.detail: The kNN search cost is asserted scalable by citation rather than measured: 'A number of extremely scalable implementations of kNN lookup are available, such as ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020) and Faiss (Johnson et al., 2021)' (lines 43-44); 'There are various other efficient approximate kNN algorithms available for CPU and GPU/TPU ... which can scale into the billions' (lines 314-315). No FLOP count, no index build time, no memory bandwidth figure for the gather. The only empirical handle on read cost is the 0.2 -> 0.25 -> 0.6 s step-time sequence.
cost_the_paper_pays_instead.source: Sec. 1 lines 42-44; Sec. 3.3 lines 311-315; Sec. 4.2 lines 496-498

models.source: Sec. 4.2, lines 478-482; param phrase at line 496; Fig. 1 x-axis tick '200M' (line 70)

training.schedule: linear warmup for the first 1000 steps, then square root decay
training.steps: 500K steps from scratch on all datasets except Isabelle; Isabelle stopped at 100K steps 'when the model began to overfit'

datasets.name: arXiv Math
datasets.provenance: AUTHOR-CONSTRUCTED. Papers downloaded via arXiv Bulk Data Access, filtered to articles labelled 'Mathematics' with LaTeX source available. 'The number of tokens per paper in this dataset is roughly comparable to the number of tokens per book in PG19, because LATEX source has many special characters and the tokenizer tends to output small subwords.' Length histogram truncated at 500K tokens; maximum paper 'almost 1.6M tokens'.

datasets.name: Github
datasets.provenance: AUTHOR-CONSTRUCTED, and constructed in a way that maximises the need for long-range lookup. BigQuery corpus of open-source repositories, filtered by file ending to C, C++, Java, Python (incl. Jupyter notebooks), Go, TypeScript. 'we created one long document for each Github repository by traversing the directory tree, and concatenating all of the files within it. The order in which files are traversed within the repository is random, but each subdirectory is processed as a unit'. Maximum repository 'just over 9M tokens'.

datasets.name: Isabelle (Formal Math)
datasets.provenance: AUTHOR-CONSTRUCTED. 'all 627 theories available on The Archive of Formal Proofs (as of October 6, 2021) and an additional 57 theories from the Isabelle standard library to create a corpus of 684 theories'. Files of a theory concatenated into one document, 'ordered according to their import dependencies, so that later files use sub-theorems that are proved in earlier files' -- i.e. the concatenation order is chosen so that the answer always precedes the question.

datasets.name: C4(4K+)
datasets.provenance: Public C4 (Raffel et al. 2020), filtered: 'We filtered out all documents that have less than 4096 tokens to focus on documents where memory can have an impact.'

datasets.name: PG-19
datasets.provenance: Public (Rae et al. 2020; Sun et al. 2021). English-language books published prior to 1919 from Project Gutenberg.

experiments.metric: Average token-level perplexity. This is the only quantitative metric in the entire paper. No downstream task, no accuracy, no generation quality measure.

Nevertheless, we still saw a substantial gain when adding an external memory of size 8192 to this model.' (2.42 -> 2.33 on arXiv)

Checked per dataset: memory-1536 (row 5) beats context-2048 (row 2) on arXiv (2.61 vs 2.69), GitHub (2.20 vs 2.22) and Isabelle (2.33 vs 2.39), but loses on PG19 (12.50 vs 12.37) and C4(4K+) (14.97 vs 14.81). We conclude that the lower layers of a Transformer don't necessarily need long-range context, and having a differentiable memory is not as important as one might suspect.'

'Increasing the size of external memory provided consistent gains up to a size of 262K. Note that 262K tokens is longer than almost all of the documents in arXiv, and thus we would not expect to see any gain past this point'

finetune_a_memoryless_model.evidence: Figure 6 only (lines 610-627, x-axis 0 / 300K / 500K / 600K training steps). No numbers tabulated.

findings: 'For the first 8192 tokens, the difference between the two models is zero, since the larger capacity of the 32K memory isn't being used yet.' (lines 653-655)

'The benefit is not universal, since the predictions for some tokens become worse, possibly due to the fact that a relevant retrieved memory no longer makes it into the top-k when the size of the external memory is increased.' (lines 655-658)

'the benefit of external memory is somewhat sparse. The improvement in perplexity seems to be mainly driven by a small percentage of tokens that obtain a large improvement in cross-entropy loss when using the larger memory.' (lines 658-660)

'we found that the model gained the most when looking up rare words, such as proper names, references, citations, and function names, where the first use of a name is too far away from subsequent uses to fit in the local context.' (lines 643-645)

random_seeds.protocol: 3 runs with 3 random seeds each, standard deviation of perplexity after 500K training steps
random_seeds.authors_reading: 'We saw the standard deviation between different runs of the same experiment appears to be much smaller than the gap between different models.' (lines 997-998)
random_seeds.note_by_this_note: This is the paper's only variance estimate and it covers exactly two configurations (Transformer-XL 512 and Memorizing Transformer with memory 8192). No error bars appear on any other number in the paper, including Fig. 1 and Fig. 6.

approximate_knn_quality.recall: 'a recall of about 90%, i.e. 90% of the true top k are returned in the approximate top k'
approximate_knn_quality.robustness_claim: 'We experimented with multiple implementations of approximate kNN lookup with different tradeoffs between quality and computational cost. We did not observe a significant degradation of the model quality when switching to lower quality approximations of kNN, so the model appears to be quite robust with respect to the quality of kNN retrieval.' -- no numbers given, no implementations named, no recall levels compared.

scale_ceiling.largest_model: 8B parameters (64 heads, 16 layers, d_model 4096, d_ff 32768), but only on arXiv Math, only at memory 8192, only at context 2048, only without XL cache, and only as a point in Figure 1 -- no perplexity for the 8B model is written down anywhere in the paper. [Sec. 4.4, lines 587-591; Fig. 1, lines 55-77]
scale_ceiling.largest_state: n_E = 262,144 (key, value) pairs per head per document, at 8 heads at one layer, reached only by finetuning for 20K steps on top of a 500K-step pretrain, and only on arXiv. Best value 2.21 at context 2048 pretrained at 65K. [Table 5, lines 510-561]. The paper itself marks this as the natural ceiling: '262K tokens is longer than almost all of the documents in arXiv, and thus we would not expect to see any gain past this point' [lines 604-605].
scale_ceiling.largest_training_run: 500K steps at 2^17 tokens per batch on 32 TPU cores = 65.536B tokens (token count DERIVED by this note; the paper states only steps and batch size). Isabelle was trained for 100K steps only, because of overfitting. [Sec. 4.2, lines 486-492]
scale_ceiling.largest_document: Github repository of 'just over 9M tokens' [Fig. 10 caption, line 936]; arXiv paper of 'almost 1.6M tokens' [Fig. 9 caption, line 933]. These are corpus statistics, not evaluated context lengths -- the model still only ever sees 512 or 2048 tokens at a time with at most 262K in E.
scale_ceiling.evaluation_ceiling: Perplexity on five language-modelling corpora, plus a 10-example hand-checked retrieval study on Isabelle. There is no downstream task anywhere: no QA, no summarisation, no code completion pass@k, no instruction following, no long-context benchmark. The strongest capability claim in the paper -- 'the model is capable of making use of newly defined functions and theorems during test time' (Abstract, lines 20-21) -- rests on that 8-out-of-10 manual inspection.
scale_ceiling.baseline_ceiling: The only baselines are the authors' own vanilla Transformer and Transformer-XL, at the same 12-layer/1024-width configuration. No retrieval baseline is run: kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al. 2020), Compressive Transformer (Rae et al. 2020), REALM, RAG, Routing Transformer, Big Bird and the rest are discussed in Sec. 2 (lines 93-205) and never reproduced.
scale_ceiling.deployment_gap: Serving is entirely out of scope. Every measurement is a training measurement; the paper contains no inference latency, no throughput, no memory footprint in bytes, no batching study at serving time, and no multi-user or multi-session scenario. The store is per document and cleared at document boundaries, so nothing in the paper speaks to a store that persists across sessions -- which is exactly what the later E-path assumes.
scale_ceiling.temporal_ceiling: March 2022. The corpus, the tokenizer (32K sentencepiece), the model scale and the hardware (TPUv3) are all pre-LLM-era; the largest model is smaller than any model in the later E-path papers of this corpus, all of which use frozen API models of unknown but far larger size.

new_concepts_introduced: kNN-augmented attention layer -- a single transformer layer that runs both dense local self-attention and approximate top-k_nn retrieval into an external store, combined by a learned gate [Sec. 3.1, lines 243-277]
non-differentiable external memory of internal (key, value) representations, written by verbatim append of the current chunk's activations [Sec. 3.1, lines 251-255]

the non-differentiability argument for scalability: because no gradient flows into E, keys and values computed under earlier parameters can be reused instead of recomputed every step [Sec. 1, lines 48-52]
staleness / distributional shift of stored keys, and key-query normalisation as its mitigation [Sec. 3.2, lines 290-306]
per-head learned scalar gate b_g between local and long-range attention, with the observation that most heads converge to memory [Eq. (1)-(2), lines 264-277]
memory-size generalisation -- train with a small n_E, deploy with a large one, optionally with 20K steps of finetuning [Sec. 1 lines 82-84; Sec. 4.5, Table 5]
retrofitting memory onto an existing memory-free checkpoint as a cheap finetune [Sec. 4.5, lines 628-635]
clearability of E as a privacy property, contrasted explicitly against Theta [Ethics, lines 763-769]
the per-token Delta cross-entropy diagnostic for locating where memory helps [Sec. 4.6, lines 648-660; Fig. 7]
extended_or_renamed: 'external memory' -- inherited from the neural-cache / Transformer-XL / memory-network line, but narrowed here to a per-head, per-document store of raw attention keys and values. In the v2 frame this is E, and the monograph must carry the standing qualifier 'representation-level E' to keep it distinct from the text-level E of MemGPT/Mem0/Letta.

'attention' -> 'information retrieval'. The paper's rhetorical move is to identify the two: 'attention acts as a form of information retrieval' (line 39), 'a simple model that unifies attention and retrieval' (line 202). This identification is what licenses the whole E-path argument at representation level.
'memory size' is redefined from bytes to tokens/pairs. Every capacity statement in this paper and in its descendants inherits this unit choice, which is exactly why the corpus has no byte numbers.

Transformer-XL's cache is re-cast as the *short-range complement* of E rather than a competitor: 'The XL cache provides additional local short-range context at the start of a sequence, which complements the long-range context provided by external memory.' (lines 575-576)
contested_or_retired: The necessity of differentiable memory. Retired explicitly: 'having a differentiable memory is not as important as one might suspect' (lines 581-582).

The necessity of compressing the carried state, as in Compressive Transformer (Rae et al. 2020). Retired by construction: 'In contrast, we use a very large cache without compression, combined with an approximate kNN attention mechanism over it.' (lines 183-184). The rate-distortion paper in this corpus later re-contests exactly this point.
The assumption that all layers need long-range context. Contested from one observation: a memory at one layer nearly matches a 4x longer differentiable context at all layers (Table 4, rows 2 and 5).
The assumption that acquiring knowledge requires moving Theta. Contested in the paper's first two sentences, without citing anyone who holds that assumption.
concepts_conspicuously_absent: sleep, consolidation, replay, catastrophic forgetting, continual learning -- zero occurrences in the whole document (verified by case-insensitive grep: 'sleep' 0, 'consolidat' 0, 'replay' 0, 'catastrophic' 0, 'continual' 0)
fast weights, Hebbian update, meta-learning, inner loop -- zero occurrences ('fast weight' 0, 'hebbian' 0, 'meta-learn' 0)
LoRA, adapter, PEFT, model editing -- zero occurrences ('adapter' 0, 'editing' 0; the single 'lora' substring hit is inside the word 'Exploration' in a bibliography entry, line 900)
any budget, amortisation, or cost-per-query vocabulary. The word 'amortiz/amortis' does not appear.

open_questions.question: What should a huge external memory actually be filled with? The paper stops at 'the same document' and hands the general case to future work.
open_questions.source: Sec. 5 Conclusion, lines 749-751: 'Unlike other forms of attention, kNN retrieval can be easily scaled up to huge memory sizes, and is thus potentially able to leverage vast knowledge bases or code repositories. How to make the best use of this capability is a topic for future work.'
open_questions.who_takes_it_up: Nobody in the E-path of this corpus takes it up at representation level. The agent-memory line answers the same question in text space (MemGPT, Mem0, ReasoningBank) without citing this paper.

open_questions.question: Should the read gate be content-dependent? The paper names the extension and does not run it.
open_questions.source: Sec. 3.1, lines 275-276: 'In our experiments, the value of the gate g does not depend on the content of the token at each position, although that would be a trivial extension to implement.'

open_questions.question: Is staleness actually the cause of the large-memory training instability, and what is its rate? Normalisation mitigates but does not eliminate it, and the causal claim is left hedged.
open_questions.source: Sec. 3.2, lines 299-306: 'Normalization does not eliminate staleness, but it at least ensures that older keys and newer keys do not differ in magnitude. ... This training instability could be due to staleness. However, models seem to be able to cope with a limited degree of staleness (with the small memory) by adjusting their queries accordingly.'

open_questions.question: Where exactly is the point of diminishing returns in n_E, and is it set by document length or by retrieval interference?
open_questions.source: Sec. 5, lines 744-745 ('Perplexity continues to improve with increasing memory size, although there is a point of diminishing returns'); Sec. 4.5 lines 604-605 attributes the arXiv ceiling to document length, while Sec. 4.6 lines 655-658 attributes per-token regressions to top-k crowding. The two explanations are never reconciled.

open_questions.question: Why do the lower layers not need long-range context? Asserted as a conclusion from one comparison, not investigated.
open_questions.source: Sec. 4.3, lines 581-582: 'We conclude that the lower layers of a Transformer don't necessarily need long-range context, and having a differentiable memory is not as important as one might suspect.'

open_questions.question: Should deletability of knowledge be an architectural requirement? The Ethics section poses the E-vs-Theta asymmetry that the entire Theta-path must later answer, and answers it only for itself.
open_questions.source: Ethics, lines 763-769: 'one advantage of using an external memory is that the memory can be easily cleared of all such information, as we do at the end of each document that we train on. The same is not true of differentiable model parameters, which is what most existing architectures use to store facts and information that they are trained on.'
open_questions.bridge_out: This is the sharpest bridge-out in the paper for the monograph's Part III: it is a 2022 statement of the exact objection that Theta-path sleep-time compute has to survive.

open_questions.question: Can this be composed with weight-level knowledge acquisition at all? Never asked. The paper sets E against Theta as alternatives and never contemplates running both.
open_questions.source: Abstract lines 10-13 frames them as alternatives; no composition experiment or discussion appears anywhere.
open_questions.bridge_out: Every hybrid in the later corpus (learned context feeding a Theta update, W folded from E) is an untaken option here.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Perplexity is the only quantitative metric in the paper. There is no downstream task of any kind -- no QA, no code completion, no summarisation, no long-context benchmark. The abstract's capability claim ('the model is capable of making use of newly defined functions and theorems during test time') is supported by a manual inspection of 10 examples, 8 of which the authors judged successful.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4 throughout; Abstract lines 20-21; Sec. 4.6 lines 726-728

unfavorable_facts.fact: The headline scaling claim -- memory worth 5X the parameters -- has no table behind it. No perplexity value for the 1B or 8B model is written down anywhere in the paper. It rests entirely on Figure 1, on one dataset (arXiv Math), at one memory size (8192), one context (2048), no XL cache, and with no error bars.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4.4 lines 585-594; Fig. 1 lines 55-77; restated in Sec. 1 lines 88-91 and Sec. 5 lines 742-744

unfavorable_facts.fact: Both qualitative studies use architectures that differ from the one all the quantitative results come from. The per-token Delta-loss analysis 'used a slightly older version of the architecture without the gating mechanism'; the Isabelle definition-retrieval case study 'used a model with two memory layers of size 32K' -- while the ablation section reports that two kNN layers give no benefit. Neither configuration appears in Table 4 or Table 5.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4.6 line 647; Sec. 4.6 lines 730-731; App. A.1 lines 955-956

unfavorable_facts.fact: The layer placement used throughout the paper is not the best one in the paper's own ablation. Layer 9 is the stated default and scores 2.37; layer 6 scores 2.36. The full sweep spans only 2.36-2.43, against a seed standard deviation of 0.005 for this model -- so the ablation resolves a 0.07 effect with a single run per point.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4.2 line 480 (default = layer 9); App. A.1 Table 14 lines 961-975; Table 16 lines 999-1008

unfavorable_facts.fact: Every ablation is run at one point in configuration space: context 512, XL cache 512, memory 8192, ~200M parameters, one dataset. No ablation is repeated at 65K memory, at context 2048, or at 1B/8B. The neighbour-count, layer-index and multi-layer conclusions are therefore single-configuration evidence.

The 'a small memory is almost as good as 4x the context' claim reverses on two of five datasets. Memory 1536 at context 512 beats context 2048 on arXiv (2.61 vs 2.69), GitHub (2.20 vs 2.22) and Isabelle (2.33 vs 2.39), but loses on PG19 (12.50 vs 12.37) and C4(4K+) (14.97 vs 14.81). The claim is stated without the per-dataset breakdown.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4.3 lines 577-579 vs Table 4 rows 2 and 5 (lines 367-464)

unfavorable_facts.fact: The staleness / instability story has no experiment behind it. It is hedged in every statement ('In some of our experiments', 'sometimes resulted in worse performance', 'could be due to staleness', 'In some cases, training was unstable', 'possibly due to distributional shift'), no unstable run is plotted or tabulated, and in the one place where the two protocols are compared at equal memory, direct training at 65K (2.31) slightly beats pretrain-8192-then-finetune-65K (2.32).
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 3.2 lines 302-306; Sec. 4.5 lines 599-601; Table 5 rows 2 and 3 (context 512)

unfavorable_facts.fact: Three of the five corpora are built by the authors, and two of them are built by concatenation procedures that manufacture the long-range dependency being measured. The Github corpus concatenates an entire repository into one document by random directory traversal; the Isabelle corpus concatenates theory files 'according to their import dependencies, so that later files use sub-theorems that are proved in earlier files' -- i.e. the definition is guaranteed to precede the reference. The largest reported gains (GitHub 3.05 -> 1.80, Isabelle 3.09 -> 1.99) are on exactly these two constructed corpora.

Table 4's caption says all models were 'trained for 500k steps', but Sec. 4.2 says Isabelle training was stopped at 100K steps because the model began to overfit. One of the five columns is therefore trained under a different protocol than the caption states.
unfavorable_facts.source: Table 4 caption line 464 vs Sec. 4.2 lines 486-488

unfavorable_facts.fact: Table 15 reports 2.38 for k_nn = 32 on the configuration Table 4 reports as 2.37. Given Table 16's +/- 0.005 seed spread for this exact model, the 0.01 gap is about 2 sigma and is never reconciled or mentioned.
unfavorable_facts.source: App. A.1 Table 15 lines 980-992 vs Table 4 row 7 arXiv column

unfavorable_facts.fact: No retrieval baseline is ever run. kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al. 2020), Compressive Transformer (Rae et al. 2020), RETRO-class retrieval, Routing Transformer, Reformer, Big Bird, Expire-span and Yogatama et al. 2021 are all discussed in Related Work and none is reproduced. The only baselines are the authors' own vanilla Transformer and Transformer-XL at the same configuration, so every reported gain is measured against the authors' own code only.

The scalability of the kNN search itself -- the paper's central efficiency argument -- is asserted by citation, not measured. ScaNN and Faiss are named as evidence that lookup 'can scale into the billions'; no index build time, no query latency, no FLOP count, no memory-bandwidth figure for the search or the gather appears. The one wall-clock number (0.2 -> 0.25 -> 0.6 s step time) shows a 3x step-time increase at 65K memory and is reported for the ~200M model only.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 1 lines 42-44; Sec. 3.3 lines 311-315; Sec. 4.2 lines 493-498

unfavorable_facts.fact: Approximate retrieval is run at ~90% recall throughout, and the claim that quality is robust to worse approximations is given with no numbers, no named implementations and no recall levels. Every headline perplexity therefore carries an unmeasured retrieval-quality confound.

Larger memory makes some tokens worse, and the paper's own explanation is unverified. 'The benefit is not universal, since the predictions for some tokens become worse, possibly due to the fact that a relevant retrieved memory no longer makes it into the top-k when the size of the external memory is increased.' The competing explanation -- FIFO eviction -- is never separated from top-k crowding, because eviction is never ablated anywhere in the paper.
unfavorable_facts.source: Sec. 4.6 lines 655-658; Sec. 3.1 lines 253-254 (eviction policy stated, never studied)

unfavorable_facts.fact: The benefit is sparse and concentrated. 'the benefit of external memory is somewhat sparse. The improvement in perplexity seems to be mainly driven by a small percentage of tokens that obtain a large improvement in cross-entropy loss.' Averaged perplexity therefore hides the shape of the win, and the fraction of tokens involved is never quantified.

Capacity is never converted to bytes or to a device footprint, even though the paper's own design multiplies it out four ways: per head (8), per document, per batch element (256 documents at context 512), at one layer. The interaction between batch size and memory size -- which is the whole serving question -- is stated as an architectural fact and never costed.

It is the sole evidence for the paper's most-quoted claim (memory worth 5X parameters) and the paper publishes no table behind it.

The architecture, and the one figure the monograph's Sec. N.3 needs: a single kNN-augmented layer near the top of the stack, the external memory of cached (key, value) pairs alongside it, and the annotation 'Will be added to external memory after the current training step' -- the write path drawn as a by-product of the read path.

The data pipeline: documents split into subsequences, one document per batch row. This is the figure that makes the serving consequence visible -- each batch row needs its own external memory, so capacity multiplies by batch size.
Retrofit curve: a pre-trained 1B memory-free Transformer finetuned to use 65K memory closes 85% of the gap in 20K steps and all of it by 100K. The E-path's cheapest-adoption argument in one plot.

Per-token Delta cross-entropy on a 22K-token paper, 8K memory vs 32K memory. Shows three things at once: the flat zero before token 8192, the sparsity of the benefit, and that some tokens get worse with more memory. The honest picture of what an averaged perplexity gain is made of.
The main result grid: 10 configurations x 5 datasets. The monograph should reproduce it whole, because the interesting reversals (memory-1536 vs context-2048) are only visible column by column.
The memory-size scaling ladder up to 262K via 20K-step finetuning, and the one place where train-at-65K and pretrain-then-finetune-to-65K can be compared.

Three Isabelle retrieval traces showing a lemma reference retrieving its own definition body from tens of thousands of tokens earlier. The qualitative core of the paper's capability claim -- print it with the n=10, 8/10 caveat attached.

Document-length histograms for all five corpora (arXiv max ~1.6M tokens, Github max just over 9M). These ground the 'no gain expected past 262K' argument and are the only place in the whole corpus where the length distribution that N_q would be drawn from is actually published.

inferences_by_this_note.inference: Byte capacity, which the paper never states. Assuming bf16 (2 bytes/elem -- the paper never states a dtype), and using its own shape (8 heads x d_head 128, keys and values both stored, one kNN layer): n_E = 1536 -> 6 MiB; 8192 -> 32 MiB; 65,536 -> 256 MiB; 262,144 -> 1 GiB. Per document.
inferences_by_this_note.arithmetic: 65536 x 8 x 128 x 2 (k and v) x 2 bytes = 268,435,456 bytes = 256 MiB
inferences_by_this_note.sanity_check: A full 12-layer KV cache for 65,536 tokens at d_model 1024 in bf16 would be 3 GiB; the kNN store is 1/12 of that because it lives at one layer. The two figures are consistent.

inferences_by_this_note.inference: Aggregate footprint at the paper's own batch sizes. Context 512 uses batch 256 documents, so at n_E = 8192 the store is 256 x 32 MiB = 8 GiB and at n_E = 65,536 it is 256 x 256 MiB = 64 GiB. Context 2048 uses batch 64, so 65,536 gives 16 GiB. The paper reports the batch sizes and the memory sizes on adjacent pages and never multiplies them.
inferences_by_this_note.ground_for_the_inputs: Sec. 4.2 lines 490-492 (batch sizes); Sec. 3.1 lines 284-285 (one memory per batch element)

inferences_by_this_note.inference: The post-retrieval gather moves 128 KiB per token per kNN layer (k_nn 32 x d_head 128 x 2 tensors x 2 bytes x 8 heads = 131,072 bytes), i.e. 64 MiB per 512-token chunk per batch element, independent of n_E. A dense scan of the whole store would move n_E x 8 x 128 x 2 x 2 bytes. The two are equal at n_E = C x k_nn = 512 x 32 = 16,384 pairs. Below that, retrieval reads MORE bytes than simply attending to everything; above it, retrieval wins, and the advantage grows linearly. The paper's smallest memory (1536) and its 8192 setting both sit below that break-even, which is a plausible byte-level reason the 8K-vs-65K step-time gap (0.25 s vs 0.6 s) is so much smaller than the 8x capacity ratio.
inferences_by_this_note.status: INFERENCE. The break-even identity is exact given the shapes; the attribution of the step-time pattern to it is speculation and must be marked as such in the chapter, or dropped.

inferences_by_this_note.inference: Shared-weight batching survives intact. Because nothing per-user is written into Theta, requests keep sharing one weight copy and the per-request state behaves exactly like a KV cache -- allocate on document start, grow to a cap, free on document end. This is the property the Theta-path forfeits. The Rosetta entry to use is 'KV cache', not 'model redeploy'.
inferences_by_this_note.ground_for_the_inputs: Sec. 3.1 lines 284-285; absence of any per-user parameter anywhere in the paper

inferences_by_this_note.inference: At 256 MiB per document per kNN layer the store does not live in on-chip SRAM; it lands in HBM, and for the billion-scale case the paper gestures at (ScaNN/Faiss, line 315) it lands in host DRAM or on disk behind an ANN index. The traffic profile is therefore a random gather over a large, mostly-cold region -- the opposite of the streaming, fully-read KV-cache access pattern the reader is used to at decode.

Because the write fires only at chunk boundaries, a generating model cannot retrieve anything it produced within the current chunk -- up to 512 (or 2048) tokens of self-generated text are invisible to E until the chunk closes. The paper never runs generation, so this never surfaces, but it is a hard constraint for any decode-time use.

Decode-time read cost is O(search) + O(k_nn x d_head) per token per head, not O(n_E) as full attention over the store would be. The search term is whatever the ANN index costs and is the only unbounded term; the paper measures neither, and its entire scalability claim rests on that unmeasured term.

systems_implications.what_the_reader_should_take_away: This is the E-path with the sleep budget set to zero. It buys long-range recall by paying in read-side gather bandwidth and per-request bytes rather than in offline compute, and it keeps the two serving properties the Theta-path gives up -- shared weights across requests, and O(1) deletion of a user's knowledge. Everything the reader would need to size it (bytes, decode latency, index cost) has to be derived; the paper supplies shapes and one step-time triple.
